New puppy — the first week

Buy less than you think. The first week is mostly routine and towels.

  • Same food the breeder was feeding — swap brands slowly over 7 days
  • Crate or bed in a quiet corner, not the busiest room
  • Collar + tag, and a lead you can hold with one hand
  • Two bowls, one for water that stays full
  • Enzyme cleaner for accidents — normal cleaner leaves the scent mark
  • Old towels by the door for wet paws
  • Chew toy and a soft toy. Not your slippers.

First 48 hours

  1. Let the pup explore one room. No crowds of visitors.
  2. Vet booked within 3 days for a check + vaccination plan.
  3. Out to toilet every 90 minutes, and after every nap, meal, play.
  4. Praise the second it finishes outside. Ten seconds late and it means nothing to them.
No dog parks until the vet says the vaccines are done.
Sleep is training. A tired puppy is a biting puppy, user_name.

Exam revision week

Seven days. Recall beats rereading — test yourself or it doesn't count.

  • Past papers printed, ideally three of them
  • One page of formulas or key facts, written by hand
  • Topic list with weak spots starred
  • Timer — 25 minutes on, 5 off
  • Phone in another room during blocks
  • Water bottle on the desk, snacks that aren't crisps
  • Sleep before midnight. Cramming at 2am costs you marks at 9am.
The seven-day shape
  • Days 1–2: cover weak topics, make short notes
  • Days 3–4: past paper, mark it, list every mistake
  • Day 5: fix those mistakes, then a second paper
  • Day 6: light review, only your one-pagers
  • Day 7: bag packed, route checked, early night
Teaching a topic out loud to an empty room is the fastest way to find the hole, user_name.

Balcony vegetable patch checklist

A patch the size of a doormat still counts. Start here.

  • Measure the sun — 6+ hours means tomatoes, 3–4 means greens.
  • Check your rail or wall can take weight before pots go up.

  • Water in the morning; balcony pots dry twice as fast as beds.
  • Feed every two weeks once flowers show up.
  • Watch for whitefly and aphids — one squirt of soapy water, repeat weekly.

Small tip: group thirstier pots together so you're not guessing which one looks sad.

Before a tattoo appointment checklist

The art lasts forever. The prep lasts a day.

  • Sleep properly the night before — tired skin hurts more.
  • Eat a real meal an hour before; low blood sugar is the enemy.
  • Hydrate, but not so much you're up mid-session.
  • Skip alcohol and painkillers that thin blood for 24 hours.
  • Wear loose clothing that leaves the area easy to reach.
  • Bring comfy layers, water, and a snack if it's a long session.
  • Shower, but no lotion or oils on the spot.
  • Confirm the design and placement with your artist once more.

Near miss: don't shave the area yourself unless asked — artists usually do it to avoid nicks.

instances.html:
Sourdough starter first week checklist

Flour, water, patience. Mostly patience.

  • Day 1: mix 50g wholemeal flour with 50g warm water in a jar.
  • Day 2: stir, look for tiny bubbles. Nothing? Normal.
  • Day 3–4: it may smell like socks or nail polish. Also normal.
  • Day 3 onward: discard all but 50g, feed 50g flour + 50g water daily.
  • Day 5–7: watch for it doubling 4–8 hours after feeding.
  • Keep it somewhere 22–26°C, out of direct sun.
  • Use a loose lid — it needs to breathe, not explode.
  • Ready when it doubles reliably and smells like yogurt.

Good sign: a domed top and a web of bubbles underneath. Bake something.

  • Review your openings once, not for an hour.
  • After each game, note one thing you'd do differently.

Small tip: between rounds, walk and breathe. Sitting still for six hours is its own opponent.

New bike helmet fit checklist

A helmet only works if it sits right. Five minutes now saves your noggin later.

  • Level it — front rim just above eyebrows, back covers the base of your skull.
  • Dial the fit — turn the rear adjuster until it's snug but not pinching.
  • Check side straps — they should form a V just below your ears.
  • Adjust chin strap — one finger should fit between strap and chin.
  • Do the shake test — open your mouth wide; helmet should press down slightly.
  • Wear it on every ride — even the quick ones. Especially the quick ones.
  • Replace after a crash — or every 5 years, whichever comes first.

If it slides around or feels loose, keep adjusting. A wobbly helmet is barely better than none.

First aquarium setup

Fish come last, user_name. The water needs a job first.

  • Pick the spot
    Away from windows and vents. Steady temperature beats a pretty view.
  • Wash substrate and decor
    Rinse gravel in a bucket until the water runs clear. Hot water only, no soap, ever.
  • Fill and dechlorinate
    Tap water is fine once treated. Dose for the full tank volume, not just what you pour.
  • Start the filter and heater
    Let both run 24 hours before anything living goes in.
  • Test water daily
    Ammonia and nitrite should climb, then fall to zero. That's the cycle doing its work.
  • Add fish slowly
    Float the bag 15 minutes, then net the fish in. Skip the shop water.

Instant Pot first run

It's a pressure cooker, user_name. Respect the valve and it's just a very patient kettle.

  • Read the valve, not the manual
    Find Sealing and Venting on the lid. That one switch explains most scary stories.
  • Run the water test
    Two cups of water, Manual 5 minutes, natural release. It proves the seal works and rinses the factory smell.
  • Never fill past two-thirds
    Half full for anything that foams, like beans or pasta.
  • Use at least one cup of liquid
    The pot needs steam to build pressure. Dry grains will scorch.
  • Plan the release
    Quick release for veg, natural for meat. Ten minutes of natural release is a good default.
  • Hand wash the lid and ring
    The silicone ring holds onto strong smells. Soak it in vinegar water now and then.

First scarf, start to finish

One stitch until it stops being interesting, user_name. Then it gets good.

  • Buy chunky yarn and size 8-10 needles
    Thin yarn and tiny needles make everything harder. Save them for scarf two.
  • Knit a practice square first
    Twenty rows you'll throw away teaches cast-on, knitting, and tension.
  • Learn cast-on and knit stitch only
    Garter stitch is just knitting every row. That's a whole scarf. You don't need more yet.
  • Cast on 20-30 stitches
    Chunky yarn, that's roughly a scarf. Count twice before row one.
  • Knit until it's as long as your person
    Six feet is generous. Five is fine. Stop when the yarn runs low.
  • Cast off loosely and weave in the tails
    Too tight and the edge puckers. Leave long tails, you'll thank yourself.

Most new plants die of enthusiasm, user_name. Do less than you want to.

  • Quarantine it for a week
    Check the undersides of leaves for bugs before it meets your collection.
  • Wait on repotting
    Let it settle. Repot only if roots are circling out of the drainage holes.
  • Find its light level
    Bright indirect for most. Right up against a window is direct, and it burns leaves.
  • Water only when the top inch is dry
    Stick a finger in. Schedules kill plants, fingertips don't.
  • Empty the saucer
    Standing water rots roots. No saucer? Water in the sink and let it drip.
  • Keep the nursery tag
    That little stick is your plant's name. You'll forget it by Friday.

Set a budget, learn the table minimums, and tip the dealers.

  • Set a time limit, not just a money limit
  • Remember: the house always has an edge. Play for fun, not for rent.
